scenario: A support agent's prerequisite gate blocks process_refund until get_customer returns a verified ID. The team is now adding a new process_exchange tool that has the same identity-verification requirement.
stem: What is the most maintainable way to extend the enforcement to the new tool?

options.text: Duplicate the verification logic inline inside process_exchange's own handler, separately from process_refund's gate.
Extend the shared prerequisite-gate mechanism to also cover process_exchange, so both tools enforce the same identity check through one reusable rule.
Add a system-prompt reminder telling the agent to verify identity before using process_exchange.
Skip enforcement for process_exchange since it doesn't move money directly.

rationale.correct: A shared, reusable prerequisite-gate mechanism that any money- or identity-sensitive tool can register with keeps enforcement centralized and consistent, rather than re-implementing (and risking a slightly different, buggy version of) the same check per tool.

distractors.A: Duplicating the logic per tool creates multiple copies to keep in sync and is exactly the maintenance burden a shared mechanism avoids.
distractors.C: A prompt reminder is probabilistic, not deterministic, and doesn't meet the bar this exam guide sets for identity/financial enforcement.
distractors.D: Exchanges still touch customer identity and account state; skipping enforcement here reopens the same misidentification risk the gate was built to close.

scenario: Refund approval thresholds differ by customer tier: standard customers need approval above $500, while premium customers are approved automatically up to $2,000.
stem: How should this tiered threshold be enforced?

options.text: A single hard-coded $500 gate for everyone, with premium customers manually overridden case by case.
A programmatic gate that looks up the customer's tier and applies the corresponding threshold before allowing process_refund to proceed.
A system-prompt instruction listing both thresholds and asking the agent to apply the correct one.
Remove the gate entirely and rely on the agent's judgment about what "seems reasonable" per tier.

rationale.correct: The enforcement mechanism should stay programmatic and deterministic even when the rule has multiple cases; a gate that looks up tier and applies the matching threshold generalizes the same guarantee to tiered policy without falling back to probabilistic prompt compliance.

distractors.A: Manual overrides for premium customers reintroduce exactly the case-by-case inconsistency a gate is meant to eliminate.
distractors.C: A prompt listing both thresholds is still probabilistic compliance and can misapply the wrong threshold under the same failure modes as a single-threshold prompt.
distractors.D: Removing enforcement entirely abandons the guarantee altogether, worse than either prior option.

scenario: A customer's message reads: 'I want to talk to a person, not a bot — also, can you tell me the status of order #4471 while I wait?'
stem: How should the agent interpret the second half of the message?

options.text: As evidence the customer doesn't actually need escalation, since they're willing to interact with the agent for the order-status question.

As a request for a quick, low-stakes status lookup made while genuinely still wanting to be handed to a human — the explicit escalation request stands, and the agent should still route to a human (optionally after supplying the order status).
As a cancellation of the earlier escalation request, since any further engagement with the agent implicitly withdraws it.
As grounds to ask the customer to clarify whether they still want a human, before doing anything else.

rationale.correct: The explicit request for a human is still the operative signal; a customer can want a quick answer while waiting without that retracting their stated preference. Escalation should proceed, and providing the order status is a reasonable courtesy alongside it, not a substitute for honoring the request.

distractors.A: Willingness to ask one more question doesn't retract an explicit, first-class escalation trigger already stated in the same message.
distractors.C: Nothing in the message actually withdraws the escalation request; treating continued engagement as automatic withdrawal isn't supported by what the customer said.
distractors.D: Asking the customer to reconfirm an already-explicit request adds friction the guide specifically warns against.

scenario: The agent acknowledges a customer's frustration about a damaged order and offers to process a reshipment now. The customer replies: 'Fine, but this had better not happen a fourth time,' without asking for a human.
stem: What should the agent do at this point?

options.text: Escalate now, since the customer's continued frustration after the first acknowledgment is itself a stronger signal than before.
Proceed with the reshipment as offered, since the customer accepted the resolution and still has not requested a human — continued frustration alone remains insufficient grounds to escalate.
Ask the customer a second time whether they'd prefer a human, since their tone hasn't improved.
Apply a service credit automatically, since repeated frustration justifies compensation regardless of what was offered or requested.

rationale.correct: The customer accepted the offered resolution and still hasn't asked for a human; persistent frustration on its own remains distinct from an escalation trigger. The agent should proceed with the accepted reshipment rather than treating tone as grounds to escalate or add unrequested friction.

distractors.A: Escalation triggers are explicit requests, policy gaps, or exhausted capability — not the intensity or persistence of frustration by itself.
distractors.C: The customer already accepted the offered path; asking again introduces friction the guide cautions against when a resolution was just accepted.
distractors.D: Compensation wasn't requested or established as policy for this situation, and offering it doesn't follow from the interaction as described.

scenario: After enriching two similar tools' descriptions with formats, examples, and disambiguating guidance, the agent still occasionally calls the wrong one for genuinely ambiguous requests.
stem: What is the appropriate next step, given the first-step remedy (better descriptions) hasn't fully resolved it?

options.text: Immediately merge the two tools into one, since any remaining confusion means they should never have been separate.
Add a few-shot example set specifically covering the genuinely ambiguous request patterns that still cause misrouting, layered on top of the improved descriptions.
Revert the description changes, since they clearly didn't work.
Add a hidden keyword-matching router in front of the model to force tool selection outside the model's own reasoning.

rationale.correct: When enriched descriptions close most but not all of the gap, targeted few-shot examples for the specific remaining ambiguous patterns are the next proportionate step — it builds on the improved descriptions rather than discarding them or reaching for a heavier-handed fix.

distractors.A: Merging is a larger architectural change that should follow, not precede, exhausting cheaper fixes like targeted examples.
distractors.C: Reverting a fix that measurably reduced (even if it didn't eliminate) misrouting discards real progress.
distractors.D: A hidden router bypasses the model's own tool-selection reasoning entirely, which is a heavier, less flexible intervention than examples for the remaining edge cases.

scenario: After a name-only lookup returns three matches, the agent asks for an order number. The customer provides one, but it still matches two of the three original accounts (a shared/family order).
stem: What should the agent do now that one additional identifier didn't fully disambiguate?

options.text: Pick either of the two remaining matches at random, since asking for a second additional identifier would be excessive after already asking once.
Ask for one more distinguishing identifier (e.g., email or billing zip code) specific to the two remaining candidates, continuing the same clarification approach rather than reverting to a guess.
Escalate to a human immediately, since needing a second round of clarification indicates the case is now too complex for the agent.
Proceed with whichever of the two accounts has the more recent activity, since recency is a reasonable tiebreaker at this point.

rationale.correct: The same principle that applied to the first ambiguity still applies: request another specific identifier that can distinguish between the remaining candidates, rather than guessing. Needing a second clarifying question doesn't change the underlying rule against acting on an unconfirmed match.

distractors.A: A random pick between two still-live candidate accounts is exactly the heuristic-guess risk the original rule exists to prevent.
distractors.C: A second round of clarification is still a proportionate response to genuine ambiguity, not evidence the case exceeds the agent's scope.
distractors.D: Recency still isn't evidence of identity; it was the wrong basis for a decision the first time and remains so on a second ambiguous match.

scenario: A single customer message to the support agent contains three distinct issues: a refund request, a wrong shipping address, and a coupon that failed to apply.
stem: What is the best way to handle it?

options.text: Resolve the first issue and ask the customer to open separate tickets for the others.
Decompose the message into three items, investigate each (in parallel where possible) using shared context, then synthesize one unified resolution.
Escalate the whole conversation because multi-issue requests exceed the agent's scope.
Address only the issue whose wording sounds most urgent.

rationale.correct: Multi-concern requests should be decomposed into distinct items, each investigated against the shared conversational context, then synthesized into a single coherent resolution that addresses all three.

distractors.A: Shifting two of the three issues back onto the customer to file separately creates unnecessary friction and is not how decomposition should work.
distractors.C: Escalating the entire conversation is disproportionate; multi-issue requests are within scope once decomposed.
distractors.D: Picking only the most urgent-sounding issue silently drops legitimate parts of the request.

scenario: A support agent escalates and hands off a summary containing the customer ID, root cause, and refund amount, but no recommended action.
stem: What is the most likely consequence of omitting the recommended action, and what should be added?

options.text: No real consequence; a human agent with the other three fields can always infer the right next step unaided.
The receiving human must re-derive what the agent already concluded should happen, slowing resolution; the handoff should include a specific recommended action.
The omission is intentional best practice, since humans should always decide the action independently of the agent's assessment.
The fix is to include the full conversation transcript instead, so the human can read everything themselves.

rationale.correct: A structured handoff's purpose is to let the human act immediately without reconstructing context. Omitting the recommended action forces them to redo reasoning the agent already performed, defeating the point of a structured summary — the fix is to add it, not to compensate with unrelated fields.

distractors.A: The other three fields describe the situation but not what to do about it; assuming the human will infer the same conclusion the agent reached is not guaranteed and reintroduces delay.
distractors.C: A recommendation from the agent doesn't remove the human's authority to decide; it's a starting point that speeds resolution, not a bypass of judgment.
distractors.D: A full transcript is exactly the unstructured, slow-to-parse alternative a structured handoff exists to avoid.

scenario: A case-facts block correctly preserves exact amounts, dates, and order numbers across a long conversation, but after many issues accumulate in one extended case, the block itself has grown large enough to consume a meaningful share of the context budget.
stem: What is the appropriate way to keep the case-facts block itself from becoming a new context problem?

options.text: Let it keep growing indefinitely, since case facts must never be dropped once captured, regardless of how large the block becomes.
Periodically prune facts that are no longer relevant to any open issue (e.g., a fully resolved and closed sub-issue's specifics), while still protecting the facts tied to currently open concerns.
Move the case-facts block into the conversation history itself, so it gets summarized along with everything else.
Cap the case-facts block at a fixed small size and drop the oldest facts first, regardless of whether they're still relevant to an open issue.

rationale.correct: The case-facts block's value is precision on facts that still matter; once a sub-issue is fully resolved, its specifics are no longer load-bearing and can be pruned, keeping the block's growth tied to genuinely open concerns rather than an ever-accumulating, unbounded record.

distractors.A: Unbounded growth defeats the purpose of a lean, precise persistent block and recreates a context-budget problem of its own.
distractors.C: Moving the facts into the summarized history reintroduces exactly the lossy-summarization risk the block was created to avoid.
distractors.D: A naive oldest-first cap risks dropping facts still tied to a currently open issue, purely based on age rather than relevance.

scenario: An engineer wants a supervisory script that flags any completed session whose last recorded response has a stop_reason other than a clean finish, so a human can review incomplete or truncated runs.
stem: Which stop_reason values should the script treat as needing review rather than a clean completion?

options.text: Only "max_tokens", since that's the only value indicating the response was cut off.
Both "tool_use" and "max_tokens" — a final stored response with "tool_use" means the loop stopped before executing an outstanding request, and "max_tokens" means generation was cut short.
"end_turn" only, since it is the value most often confused with a genuine completion.
None of them — a script should trust the presence of a final assistant message alone, regardless of stop_reason.

rationale.correct: A stored final response with stop_reason: "tool_use" means the loop stopped without ever executing (or continuing past) a pending tool call — a sign the process was interrupted or crashed, not that it finished cleanly. "max_tokens" means the response was truncated mid-generation. Both are legitimate review triggers; "end_turn" (and a configured "stop_sequence") represent the model choosing to stop on its own terms and don't need review.

distractors.A: max_tokens alone misses the tool_use case, which is an equally strong signal that the run didn't finish as intended.
distractors.C: end_turn is exactly the normal, clean completion signal the script should NOT flag — flagging it would generate constant false alarms.
distractors.D: The presence of a final assistant message says nothing about whether the run actually completed; stop_reason is the field that distinguishes a clean finish from a truncated or interrupted one.

scenario: A stack trace points to a single function, and the proposed fix is a one-line guard clause. However, the same function is called from three different call sites, each of which needs a different fallback value when the guard triggers.
stem: Does this remain a direct-execution case, or does it warrant plan mode?

options.text: It's still direct execution — one function, one file, so complexity is inherently low regardless of caller behavior.
It warrants at least a brief planning step, since the fix now involves a design decision (three different fallback behaviors) rather than a single unambiguous change.
It should always be plan mode, since any change with more than one caller is by definition a multi-file, architectural change.
It should be skipped entirely and left as a known issue, since it's now too complicated for a quick fix.

rationale.correct: The presence of a genuine design decision — three call sites needing different fallback behavior — is what determines the mode, not merely how many files or lines are touched. A brief planning step to decide each fallback is warranted even though the change footprint is still small.

distractors.A: File count alone doesn't capture the complexity here; the decision about differing fallback values is the actual driver.
distractors.C: Multiple callers alone doesn't make something architectural; the deciding factor is whether there's a genuine unresolved design choice, which is present here but wouldn't be in every multi-caller case.
distractors.D: The complexity is a design decision to resolve, not a reason to defer the fix indefinitely.

scenario: A migration touches 45 files across three distinct modules, each with different usage patterns of the deprecated library.
stem: What is the most effective way to structure the planning itself?

options.text: One single plan-mode pass covering all 45 files uniformly, since they all involve the same underlying migration.
A plan-mode pass per module, since each module's usage patterns may call for different specific migration steps despite sharing the same overall library change.
Skip planning for two of the three modules since they are smaller, and only plan the largest one.
Plan once for the first module encountered, then apply that exact plan verbatim to the other two without further analysis.

rationale.correct: Different usage patterns per module mean the specific migration steps may genuinely differ even though the overall goal (replace the deprecated library) is shared; planning each module lets those real differences surface before code changes, rather than assuming one plan fits all three.

distractors.A: A single uniform pass risks missing module-specific usage differences that call for different specific steps.
distractors.C: Skipping planning for modules just because they're smaller ignores that usage-pattern differences, not size, are what drive the need to plan.
distractors.D: Applying one module's plan verbatim to others assumes their usage patterns match, which the scenario says they don't.

scenario: A team's shared /deploy command in .claude/commands/ works for everyone, but one engineer wants to add a few personal extra safety checks on top of it for their own local runs, without changing the shared version teammates rely on.
stem: What is the recommended way to layer a personal variant on top of a shared command?

options.text: Edit the shared .claude/commands/deploy.md directly to add the extra checks, since that file already ships with the repo.
Create a personal command with a different name in ~/.claude/commands/ that wraps or extends the shared behavior for this engineer's own use.
Ask every teammate to individually decide whether they want the extra checks, edited into the same shared file.
There is no supported way to have both; the engineer must choose either the shared command or a fully separate personal one with no relationship to it.

rationale.correct: A personal, differently-named command in the user-level ~/.claude/commands/ directory lets one engineer layer their own extra checks without touching the shared, version-controlled command everyone else depends on.

distractors.A: Editing the shared file directly imposes one engineer's personal preference on the whole team.
distractors.C: Baking an individual's preference into the shared file conflates personal and team configuration instead of separating them.
distractors.D: A personal command can still be designed to build on or reference the shared one's intent; this isn't an all-or-nothing choice.

scenario: A team's root CLAUDE.md documents a shared testing convention. One engineer also has a personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md with unrelated formatting preferences. A new teammate reports that Claude follows the testing convention but seems unaware of an unwritten 'always confirm before deleting files' habit the original engineer has relied on.
stem: What is the most likely explanation for the missing 'confirm before deleting' behavior?

options.text: That habit was never actually written into either CLAUDE.md file — it existed only as the original engineer's manual practice, not as configuration at all.
It must be in the personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and failed to propagate, the same failure mode as any user-level instruction.
Claude Code only loads one CLAUDE.md file per session, so the personal file's instructions were silently dropped in favor of the project file.
The new teammate needs to run /compact to load the missing instruction.

rationale.correct: If the behavior only ever existed as the original engineer's manual habit and was never actually written into any CLAUDE.md, there is no configuration file — user- or project-level — for a new teammate to be missing. The fix is to write it down (in the project file, if it should be shared), not to look for a propagation bug.

distractors.B: This assumes the habit was written into the personal file at all, which isn't established — it may never have been captured as an instruction anywhere.
distractors.C: Claude Code loads multiple applicable memory files together (e.g., project and user-level); it does not restrict itself to just one.
distractors.D: /compact summarizes conversation history and has no role in loading configuration files.

scenario: You provided two clear input/output examples for a normalize_address helper, and Claude's output now matches both examples exactly. On a third, unseen input with a format neither example covered, the transformation is unpredictable.
stem: What should you do next?

options.text: Add a third example covering a case near the one that failed, since more examples always resolve any remaining ambiguity.
Give up on the transformation as too ambiguous to specify.

Use the interview pattern to have Claude surface the specific edge cases and rules it's uncertain about, since the two examples pinned down what they covered but didn't establish general rules for unseen formats.
Lower the temperature, since the inconsistency is a randomness problem, not a specification problem.

rationale.correct: Two examples successfully pinned down the cases they cover but don't necessarily generalize to unseen formats — that's a sign of an underlying rule that hasn't been made explicit, which is exactly what the interview pattern surfaces by having Claude ask about the specific gaps rather than guessing.

distractors.A: More examples can help, but only if they target the actual gap; a scattershot approach doesn't guarantee covering the next unseen case any better than the last two did.
distractors.B: Genuinely specifiable problems shouldn't be abandoned; the interview pattern is designed for exactly this kind of unresolved ambiguity.
distractors.D: Temperature affects sampling variability, not whether the underlying transformation rule has been adequately communicated.

scenario: A developer already has a fairly detailed written spec for a caching layer, covering invalidation and cache-stampede handling, but is unsure whether anything domain-specific is still missing.
stem: Is the interview pattern still the right technique here, given the spec is already fairly thorough?

options.text: No — since a written spec already exists, the interview pattern is redundant and should be skipped entirely.
Yes — even a thorough spec can miss domain-specific considerations the author didn't think to write down, and the interview pattern is specifically designed to surface exactly those unknown gaps.
No — the interview pattern is only appropriate when no spec exists at all.
Yes — the interview pattern should replace the written spec entirely rather than supplement it.

rationale.correct: A written spec captures what the author already thought to specify; it does not guarantee coverage of considerations the author didn't anticipate. The interview pattern's value is precisely in surfacing those unknown unknowns, which a thorough-but-still-authored spec doesn't rule out.

distractors.A: A spec existing doesn't mean it's complete; the interview pattern targets exactly the gap a self-authored spec can't self-diagnose.
distractors.C: The technique isn't gated on the absence of any spec — it complements one, testing it against considerations the author may have missed.
distractors.D: The interview pattern surfaces gaps in a spec; it doesn't need to replace a spec that's otherwise doing useful work.

scenario: A review surfaces three issues in a data pipeline: (1) a retry count that's hard-coded instead of configurable, (2) a race condition where two issues — a shared counter increment and a missing lock — jointly cause corrupted totals, and (3) the missing lock also independently causes a rare deadlock unrelated to the counter.
stem: How should these be grouped for the fix instructions?

options.text: All three in one message, since they all touch the same file.

The counter-increment and missing-lock issues together in one message (since they jointly cause the corruption), the hard-coded retry count as a separate, independent message; the deadlock should be folded into whichever message is sent first.

The counter-increment and missing-lock issues together in one message; the hard-coded retry count separately; the deadlock addressed together with the missing lock, since both stem from the same missing-lock root cause.
Each issue in its own separate message, since batching risks confusing the model regardless of whether issues interact.

rationale.correct: The counter/lock pair interacts and should be fixed jointly so the model reasons about them together. The retry count is unrelated and can be handled separately. The deadlock shares its root cause (the missing lock) with the corruption issue, so it belongs in that same message rather than being arbitrarily attached to whichever message happens to go first.

distractors.A: Grouping by file rather than by actual interaction ignores that the retry count doesn't interact with the other two at all.
distractors.B: Folding the deadlock into 'whichever message is sent first' is arbitrary; it belongs specifically with the missing-lock fix since they share a root cause, not with an unrelated batch by convenience.
distractors.D: Splitting every issue into its own message loses the benefit of joint reasoning for the counter/lock pair, which genuinely interact.

scenario: Configuration files matching *.config.ts are scattered across many packages in a repository, and the team wants Claude to automatically apply one convention to all of them regardless of directory.
stem: What is the most maintainable approach?

options.text: Create a .claude/rules/ file with YAML frontmatter whose paths glob is **/*.config.ts.
Place a CLAUDE.md in each package directory describing the convention.
Create a skill developers invoke manually when editing config files.
Add one large section to the root CLAUDE.md and rely on Claude to infer when it applies.

rationale.correct: Glob-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ apply automatically by file pattern across any directory, which is exactly what's needed for files scattered across packages.

distractors.B: A CLAUDE.md per package is directory-bound and requires duplicating and maintaining the convention in every package.
distractors.C: A manually invoked skill requires developers to remember to run it — it isn't automatic.
distractors.D: Relying on inference from one large, monolithic root file is unreliable compared to an explicit glob-scoped rule.

scenario: You want a `security-scan` skill to run automatically whenever Claude judges that a change touches security-sensitive code, without anyone needing to remember to invoke it by name.
stem: What determines whether Claude invokes this skill automatically?

options.text: The quality and specificity of the skill's `description` field, since Claude decides whether to invoke a skill by matching the current context against its description.
Setting `disable-model-invocation: true` in the skill's frontmatter.
Adding `context: fork` so the skill activates during any security-relevant reasoning step.
Adding an `argument-hint` describing when the skill applies.

rationale.correct: Skills are triggered by Claude matching the ongoing conversation and task against the skill's description — unlike a slash command, which requires the user to explicitly type it. A clear, specific description that states what the skill does and when it applies is what drives automatic invocation.

distractors.B: `disable-model-invocation: true` does the opposite of what's wanted here — it disables automatic triggering, forcing the skill to be invoked manually only.
distractors.C: `context: fork` controls whether the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context, not whether or when it gets invoked.
distractors.D: `argument-hint` only affects the hint shown when a user manually invokes the skill as a slash command; it has no bearing on automatic invocation.

scenario: A developer investigated a large codebase in a named session, then made substantial code changes, so the file contents captured in that session's tool results are now stale.
stem: What is the most reliable way to continue the work?

options.text: Resume the prior session with --resume and keep going.
Fork the session to create a branch from the prior analysis.
Start a new session and inject a structured summary of prior findings, noting which files changed.
Increase the context window so the stale results don't get dropped.

rationale.correct: When prior tool results are stale, starting fresh and injecting a structured summary of what was found (and what changed) is more reliable than resuming, which would carry the stale results forward as if they were still current.

distractors.A: Resuming with --resume keeps the stale tool results in context, exactly the problem to avoid.
distractors.B: Forking also inherits the stale baseline from the prior session.
distractors.D: A larger context window preserves the stale data rather than correcting it.

scenario: A coordinator agent is supposed to delegate to search, document-analysis, synthesis, and report subagents, but it never delegates — it attempts every step itself.
stem: What is the most likely configuration problem?

options.text: The coordinator's allowedTools does not include "Task."
The subagents are missing system prompts.
tool_choice is set to "any."
The coordinator's max_tokens is too low to delegate.

rationale.correct: Subagents are spawned via the Task tool, so the coordinator can only invoke them if its allowedTools includes "Task"; without it, the coordinator has no way to delegate at all.

distractors.B: Missing subagent system prompts would affect subagent quality once invoked, not whether the coordinator can spawn them in the first place.
distractors.C: tool_choice governs whether/which tool must be called on a given turn; it doesn't control which tools are available.
distractors.D: max_tokens limits output length and doesn't govern the ability to invoke a tool.

scenario: Your system has three registered subagent types: `web-researcher` (broad web search), `document-analyzer` (structured extraction from provided documents), and `fact-checker` (narrow, single-claim verification). The coordinator receives a request to verify one specific statistic against an already-provided report.
stem: Which subagent type should the coordinator invoke, and why?

options.text: `fact-checker`, because the task is a narrow, single-claim verification against material already on hand, not open-ended research or general document extraction.
`web-researcher`, because verification tasks should always default to the broadest-capability subagent available.
`document-analyzer`, because any task involving a report should go to the subagent whose name mentions documents, regardless of the specific task.
All three, in parallel, so their outputs can be cross-checked against each other.

rationale.correct: Matching the task's actual shape — a narrow, single-claim check against material already provided — to the subagent type built for exactly that (`fact-checker`) is more precise and efficient than defaulting to a broader-capability agent or picking by superficial name association.

distractors.B: Defaulting to the broadest subagent regardless of task shape wastes capability and doesn't reflect how subagent types should be selected.
distractors.C: Picking by keyword match on the subagent's name rather than the actual task ignores what each type is actually built to do.
distractors.D: Invoking all three in parallel for a single simple verification is wasteful; the task doesn't call for multiple perspectives, just one targeted check.

scenario: Researching ‘the state of renewable energy,’ every subagent in a research pipeline succeeds, yet the final reports cover only solar. The coordinator's logs show it decomposed the topic into ‘solar panel efficiency,’ ‘solar farm economics,’ and ‘residential solar,’ omitting wind, hydro, and geothermal.
stem: What is the root cause?

options.text: The search subagent's queries are not comprehensive enough.
The coordinator's task decomposition is too narrow, so subagent assignments miss whole domains of the topic.
The synthesis subagent is dropping non-solar findings.
The document-analysis subagent's relevance criteria are too restrictive.

rationale.correct: The logs implicate the coordinator directly: it never assigned wind, hydro, or geothermal subtopics in the first place, so downstream subagents executed correctly on an incomplete plan.

distractors.A: The search subagent only ran the queries it was assigned; it wasn't asked about wind, hydro, or geothermal at all.
distractors.C: There's nothing to drop — synthesis never received non-solar findings because they were never researched.
distractors.D: Document-analysis correctly analyzed the documents it was given; it was never asked to look at other energy types.

scenario: A coordinator needs a synthesis subagent to combine findings, but synthesis can only meaningfully begin once the search and document-analysis subagents have both completed their work on the same topic.
stem: How should the coordinator sequence these three subagent invocations?

options.text: Spawn search and document-analysis in parallel (since they're independent of each other), then spawn synthesis afterward, once both have returned results to pass into its prompt.
Spawn all three in parallel in a single response, since parallel spawning always minimizes latency regardless of task dependencies.
Spawn them one at a time in an arbitrary order, since Task tool calls must always run sequentially.
Spawn synthesis first so it's ready to receive results as they arrive.

rationale.correct: Parallelizing only applies to genuinely independent work; search and document-analysis don't depend on each other, so they can run in parallel, but synthesis depends on both of their outputs and must wait until it has real content to synthesize.

distractors.B: Parallel spawning helps only when the spawned tasks are actually independent; spawning synthesis before its inputs exist wastes the call since it would have nothing to synthesize.
distractors.C: Task tool calls are not required to run strictly sequentially — independent ones can and should be parallelized; the constraint here is data dependency, not a blanket sequencing rule.
distractors.D: Spawning synthesis before its dependencies have produced anything gives it no findings to work with.

scenario: A research system's claim-source mappings correctly preserve attribution through synthesis. Weeks later, one cited source is discovered to have been retracted by its publisher after the report was generated.
stem: What does the existing claim-source mapping design let the team do that a report without structured attribution would not?

options.text: Nothing additional; structured attribution only helps at synthesis time, not after a report has already shipped.

Precisely identify every claim in the shipped report that depended on the retracted source, so those specific claims (and only those) can be flagged or revisited, rather than needing to re-examine the entire report.
Automatically and silently correct the retracted claims without any human review.
Prevent the source from ever having been retracted in the first place.

rationale.correct: Because each claim is explicitly tied to its source, a later problem with one source (like a retraction) can be traced to exactly the claims that depended on it — a targeted, traceable follow-up that a report without structured attribution couldn't support without re-reviewing everything from scratch.

distractors.A: The traceability structured attribution provides doesn't expire at synthesis time; it's exactly what makes a later audit like this possible.
distractors.C: Structured attribution supports identifying affected claims; it doesn't itself make a correctness judgment or replace human review of what to do about them.
distractors.D: Attribution structure has no bearing on whether an external publisher retracts a source; it only affects how traceable the consequences are.

scenario: Three credible sources report a metric: two report figures within 2% of each other, and a third reports a figure 40% higher than the other two.
stem: Does the two-source agreement change how the synthesis agent should handle the outlier, compared to a simple two-source disagreement?

options.text: Yes — with two sources agreeing, the synthesis agent should simply drop the outlier and report only the agreed-upon figure as if no conflict existed.

No in substance — the agent should still present all three figures with attribution and annotate the discrepancy, though it can note that two of the three are mutually consistent as part of that annotation, rather than silently discarding the outlier.
Yes — majority agreement among sources is sufficient grounds to treat the third source as definitively wrong and exclude it from the report entirely.
No — the agent should average all three figures into a single blended number to resolve the conflict.

rationale.correct: Two sources agreeing doesn't establish that the third is factually wrong — it could reflect a different methodology or timeframe. The agent should still preserve all three with attribution, annotating that two are mutually consistent as useful context, rather than silently dropping or definitively excluding the outlier.

distractors.A: Dropping the outlier silently discards information the reader may need, exactly as a two-source disagreement would.
distractors.C: Numeric agreement among sources isn't proof of correctness; the third source may reflect a legitimate methodological or temporal difference not yet understood.
distractors.D: Averaging in a third figure produces a number none of the three sources actually reported and still hides the underlying disagreement.

scenario: Subagent outputs already include collection dates in their structured fields. Despite this, a synthesis report still flags two same-metric figures from 2022 and 2024 as 'contradictory' without noting the year difference.
stem: Given that dates are already captured, what is the correct next fix?

options.text: Add dates to the structured output, since that is always the fix for this class of problem.

Explicitly instruct the synthesis step to compare available date/collection metadata before labeling any two figures as contradictory, since the dates being present in the data doesn't guarantee the synthesis reasoning step actually uses them.
Remove all older data from consideration, since only the most recent figure should ever be reported.
Add a conflict_detected boolean field, since that will resolve the misclassification on its own.

rationale.correct: The dates are already captured, so the gap has moved downstream: the synthesis step isn't using the metadata it has. The fix is to explicitly direct synthesis to check temporal metadata before calling two figures contradictory — capturing the data was necessary but not, on its own, sufficient.

distractors.A: Dates are already present in this scenario; re-adding data that already exists doesn't address why synthesis isn't using it.
distractors.C: Discarding older data throws away legitimate historical figures and doesn't address the actual reasoning gap.
distractors.D: A boolean flag doesn't supply reasoning about temporal context; it's a label, not the comparison the synthesis step still needs to perform.

scenario: A coordinator's iterative refinement loop has already run three re-delegation rounds on a market-research report, and each round still finds a subtopic that could be slightly deeper.
stem: What should determine when the coordinator stops iterating rather than continuing indefinitely?

options.text: Always run exactly one refinement round regardless of the findings, to bound cost.
Continue until every subtopic is exhaustively covered, since more depth is always better for a research report.
Stop once remaining gaps fall below a defined sufficiency bar (e.g., minor detail rather than a missing subtopic), balancing coverage against diminishing returns.
Never re-delegate more than once per subtopic, regardless of how thin the resulting coverage is.

rationale.correct: Iterative refinement should continue only while it is closing meaningful gaps; once remaining gaps are minor rather than substantive, further rounds cost more than they add. A defined sufficiency bar keeps the loop from running indefinitely on marginal improvements.

distractors.A: A fixed one-round rule ignores whether that round actually closed the gaps; some reports need more, others need none.
distractors.B: Exhaustive coverage has no natural stopping point and would make the loop run indefinitely at unbounded cost.
distractors.D: Capping re-delegation at one attempt per subtopic regardless of outcome can leave a real gap unresolved even when one more targeted pass would close it.

scenario: You want to find every `TODO` comment left in the codebase before a release, regardless of which file or language they're in.
stem: Which built-in tool is the right choice?

options.text: Grep for the string `TODO`.
Glob with a pattern like `**/*.md`.
Read every file and scan visually for `TODO`.
Bash with a recursive `ls`.

rationale.correct: Grep searches file contents for a text pattern regardless of file type or location, which is exactly what's needed to find every occurrence of a comment marker like `TODO` across the whole codebase.

distractors.B: Glob only matches file paths/names by pattern; `**/*.md` would also incorrectly restrict the search to markdown files, missing TODOs in code.
distractors.C: Reading every file to scan manually is far less efficient than a single targeted content search.
distractors.D: A recursive directory listing enumerates file paths; it doesn't search inside file contents at all.

scenario: You need to find every `Dockerfile` in a monorepo containing dozens of services, regardless of how deeply nested each service's directory is.
stem: Which built-in tool fits best?

options.text: Grep for the string "FROM" (a line every Dockerfile contains).
Glob with `**/Dockerfile`.
Read the top-level directory listing.
Bash with `find` piped through several `grep` stages.

rationale.correct: Glob matches files by name/path pattern regardless of nesting depth; `**/Dockerfile` finds every file with that exact name at any depth, which is exactly the naming-convention search this calls for.

distractors.A: Searching for a common line like `FROM` searches contents, and risks false positives/negatives depending on file conventions — it's solving the wrong problem when the actual ask is finding files by name.
distractors.C: The top-level listing won't surface Dockerfiles nested inside each service's own subdirectory.
distractors.D: Chaining `find` and `grep` through Bash reinvents what Glob already does directly and more reliably.

scenario: You need to run the project's existing test suite (`npm test`) and view the output to confirm a fix works.
stem: Which built-in tool is appropriate here?

options.text: Bash, to execute the existing test command directly.
Edit, to modify the test files so they print their own results.
Grep, to search test files for assertions.
Write, to create a new test-runner script from scratch.

rationale.correct: Running an existing shell command like a test suite is exactly what Bash is for — it executes commands and returns their output, with no need to touch any files at all.

distractors.B: Editing test files to change how they print doesn't run them, and needlessly modifies source you don't need to touch.
distractors.C: Grep searches file contents; it can't execute anything or report live test results.
distractors.D: Writing a brand-new runner from scratch reinvents infrastructure that already exists and works.

scenario: A developer needs to build an accurate mental model of a large, unfamiliar codebase before making changes.
stem: What is the best strategy for building understanding of a large, unfamiliar codebase?

options.text: Read all files upfront to load complete context before answering questions.
Start with Grep to find entry points, then use Read to follow imports and trace flows incrementally.
Ask the agent to summarize the codebase from typical patterns for that kind of project.
Glob every file and Read them in alphabetical order.

rationale.correct: Incremental exploration — Grep for entry points, then Read to follow imports and trace flows — builds accurate understanding without exhausting the context window.

distractors.A: Reading everything upfront wastes context and dilutes attention across mostly-irrelevant files.
distractors.C: Relying on ‘typical patterns’ for the project type invents details instead of reading the actual code.
distractors.D: Reading every file in alphabetical order has the same context-exhaustion problem as reading everything upfront, without even prioritizing relevance.

scenario: You're designing an MCP server for a wiki. Some data is quasi-static reference material (the page index, category taxonomy) that rarely changes; other functionality requires the agent to actively search page content by keyword, or create and update pages.
stem: How should you split this between MCP resources and MCP tools?

options.text: Expose the static page index and category taxonomy as resources (so the agent can see them without a tool call), and expose search, create, and update actions as tools (since those require dynamic input the agent supplies each time).
Expose everything as tools, since tools are the only mechanism MCP provides for making data available to an agent.
Expose everything as resources, including search and update actions, so the agent has full visibility with no tool-calling overhead.
Expose the page index as a tool the agent calls once per session, and put search/update behind resources instead.

rationale.correct: Resources are the right fit for stable, browsable reference content the agent should have visibility into without spending a tool call — exactly the page index and taxonomy here. Actions that need per-call, dynamic input (a search query, new page content) are what tools are for.

distractors.B: Tools aren't the only mechanism — that's exactly the design flaw resources exist to fix, and using tools for stable reference data adds needless exploratory calls.
distractors.C: Search and update are actions with per-call inputs and side effects (for update); resources are read-only content, not a substitute for actions.
distractors.D: This inverts the correct assignment — the stable index is what benefits from resource-style visibility, and the dynamic actions are what need tool semantics.

scenario: A coding agent keeps using the built-in Grep tool instead of a team's more capable MCP code-search tool.
stem: What is the best fix?

options.text: Remove the agent's access to Grep entirely.
Enhance the MCP tool's description to clearly explain its capabilities and outputs so the agent prefers it.
Rename the built-in Grep tool.
Force tool_choice to the MCP tool on every turn.

rationale.correct: Enhancing the MCP tool's description so its capabilities and outputs are clear leads the model to prefer it over the built-in when it's genuinely the better choice, addressing the root cause of the selection problem.

distractors.A: Removing Grep entirely is heavy-handed and removes a tool that's still useful for some turns.
distractors.C: Renaming Grep doesn't communicate anything about the MCP tool's actual value.
distractors.D: Forcing tool_choice to the MCP tool on every turn is inflexible for turns where Grep is genuinely the better fit.

scenario: A well-known community MCP server for your CRM hasn't been updated in two years, has several open security issues, and doesn't support your CRM's newer API version, which your team needs.
stem: Given the general guidance to prefer community servers for standard integrations, what should you do here?

options.text: Build (or fork and update) a custom server anyway, since an unmaintained, insecure, or feature-incomplete community server no longer represents the low-risk, well-solved option the general guidance assumes.
Use the community server as-is, since community servers should always be preferred over custom ones regardless of their maintenance state.
Skip MCP entirely and call the CRM's REST API directly from the agent.
Expose the CRM only as an MCP resource, with no tools, to avoid the security issues.

rationale.correct: The 'prefer community servers' guidance is a default for well-maintained, standard integrations — it assumes reasonable security and feature parity. When a community server is stale, insecure, or missing needed capabilities, those assumptions no longer hold, and building or updating a custom server is the right call.

distractors.B: Treating 'prefer community' as an absolute rule ignores the very problems described — an outdated, insecure, or incomplete server is not actually the safe default anymore.
distractors.C: Bypassing MCP entirely loses the standardized tool-discovery and integration benefits MCP provides, and doesn't address the underlying need for a properly integrated server.
distractors.D: A resource-only exposure can't perform the write/update actions CRM work typically requires, and doesn't solve the security or version gaps either.

scenario: An agent legitimately needs access to most of an 18-tool platform across different request types, but selection reliability suffers whenever all 18 are available at once.
stem: What design best preserves broad capability while restoring selection reliability?

options.text: Keep all 18 tools available on every turn and accept the selection-reliability cost as unavoidable.
Classify each incoming request by type first, then expose only the subset of tools relevant to that request type for the turn.
Remove least-used tools permanently, regardless of whether some request types still need them.
Add few-shot examples covering all 18 tools to compensate.

rationale.correct: Dynamically scoping which tools are exposed per request type keeps the full capability available across the system while never presenting the model with more choices than a given turn actually needs — directly addressing the decision-complexity problem instead of trading away capability or patching around it.

distractors.A: Accepting the cost when a structural fix is available ignores a well-understood, addressable problem.
distractors.C: Permanently removing tools some request types still need trades away real capability instead of fixing the selection problem.
distractors.D: Examples for all 18 tools add prompt overhead without reducing the decision complexity of choosing among that many options on a single turn.

scenario: Ten minutes into a brand-new session with almost no prior exploration yet, an agent answers a question about a specific class by describing 'typical patterns for this kind of service' instead of the actual class.
stem: Is this the same context-degradation signature described elsewhere, and does a scratchpad file fix it?

options.text: Yes to both — any 'typical patterns' phrasing is context degradation by definition, and a scratchpad always resolves it.

No — with almost no session history yet, there's little context to have degraded; the more likely cause is that the agent hasn't actually explored the specific class yet, so grep/read the actual code first rather than reaching for a scratchpad.
Yes, but the fix is different — restart the session entirely rather than using a scratchpad.
No — this indicates the model is fundamentally incapable of understanding the codebase, regardless of session length.

rationale.correct: Context degradation describes specific findings getting diluted or pushed out over a long session; ten minutes into a fresh session with minimal history, there isn't much to have degraded. Falling back to general patterns this early more likely means the code hasn't actually been read yet — the fix is incremental exploration (grep then read), not a scratchpad meant for a different problem.

distractors.A: The phrasing alone doesn't establish the cause; session length and prior investigation depth matter, and both are minimal here.
distractors.C: Restarting a session that's already only ten minutes old addresses nothing, since there's little accumulated context to lose either way.
distractors.D: A capability conclusion isn't supported by an agent simply not yet having explored a specific file it hasn't been directed to yet.

scenario: A CI job already runs claude -p "Review this PR", yet the job still occasionally hangs on certain PRs.
stem: Given that -p is already correctly used, what is the most likely remaining cause of the hang?

options.text: -p doesn't actually prevent interactive prompts in all cases, so the fix is to abandon it and find another flag.
A tool the review invokes (e.g., a custom script or MCP server call) is itself waiting on interactive input or an external resource, independent of Claude Code's own print-mode behavior.
The CI runner's timeout is set too low, which is unrelated to hanging at all.
-p requires a companion --non-interactive flag that this job is missing.

rationale.correct: Once -p correctly puts Claude Code itself into non-interactive mode, a persistent hang is more likely coming from something Claude Code calls out to — a tool, script, or external service still waiting on input or a slow/blocked resource — rather than from Claude Code's own prompt handling.

distractors.A: -p is the documented, correct mechanism; abandoning it because a hang persists elsewhere misdiagnoses the cause.
distractors.C: A too-low timeout would cause the job to fail fast, not hang indefinitely — that's the opposite symptom.
distractors.D: There is no separate required companion flag; -p is the complete non-interactive invocation.

scenario: A CI review currently posts inline comments using --output-format json and --json-schema. The team wants to add a new confidence field to every finding without breaking the existing downstream parser that only recognizes the original fields.
stem: What is the safest way to introduce the new field?

options.text: Add confidence as a new optional field in the JSON schema, and update the downstream parser to read it while still tolerating its absence from any not-yet-updated callers.
Remove --json-schema entirely so the field can be added freely without schema constraints.
Post two separate sets of findings — one with the old schema, one with the new — and let the downstream code pick whichever it prefers.
Rename the existing fields to make room for the new one, since JSON objects have a fixed number of keys.

rationale.correct: Adding a new field as optional in the schema is backward compatible: existing parsers that don't yet know about confidence are unaffected, since strict schema enforcement continues to guarantee the fields those parsers do expect, while newer parser code can opt in to reading the addition.

distractors.B: Removing schema enforcement reopens the exact reliability problem --json-schema was adopted to solve.
distractors.C: Maintaining two parallel output formats doubles complexity for no benefit over a single backward-compatible schema addition.
distractors.D: JSON objects don't have a fixed key count; renaming existing fields would break every current consumer for no reason.

scenario: A team's code-review prompt for self-review already says, in bold, 'Be maximally critical and assume there are bugs, even if the code looks correct to you.' The same session still misses the same class of bugs it introduced.
stem: Why does strengthening the self-review instruction not fix this?

options.text: The instruction wasn't strong enough; an even more emphatic version would resolve it.

The limitation isn't about instruction strength — the session retains the reasoning that produced the code, and that retained context, not weak wording, is what makes it less likely to challenge its own prior decisions.
This means self-review should never be attempted in any form.
The instruction needs to be moved from the user prompt into the system prompt to take effect.

rationale.correct: No amount of emphatic wording changes what the model already has in context — its own generation reasoning, which it still treats as settled. The fix that actually addresses this is an independent review instance without that inherited context, not a stronger version of the same in-session instruction.

distractors.A: Escalating the wording doesn't change the underlying cause (retained context), so it wouldn't be expected to help regardless of emphasis.
distractors.C: Self-review isn't useless — it's just insufficient as a substitute for a genuinely independent instance; the guide doesn't recommend abandoning review, it recommends restructuring it.
distractors.D: Prompt placement doesn't remove the retained reasoning context that's the actual limitation here.

scenario: A team added a cross-file integration pass on top of their per-file passes, but it still misses a bug where one file's function signature change silently breaks a caller in another file, because the integration pass is currently just re-running the same per-file prompt across all files at once.
stem: What is missing from the integration pass as currently implemented?

options.text: Nothing; simply running the per-file prompt across all files together already constitutes a correct integration pass.

The integration pass needs its own distinct focus — explicitly reasoning about data flow and contracts between files (e.g., changed signatures and their call sites) — rather than reusing the per-file prompt's local-issue focus at a wider scope.
The fix is to increase the model's context window so all files fit even more comfortably.
The fix is to run the per-file pass a second time on every file, in addition to the first pass.

rationale.correct: An integration pass that just reruns the per-file prompt across more files at once still asks the same local questions, not the cross-file question. It needs a distinct prompt/focus specifically on data flow and contracts between files to catch the kind of signature-change bug described.

distractors.A: Running the same local-focused prompt at a wider scope doesn't introduce reasoning about cross-file contracts, which is exactly what's missing.
distractors.C: A larger context window doesn't itself introduce cross-file reasoning if the prompt never asks for it.
distractors.D: Repeating the same per-file prompt a second time doesn't add the missing focus; it just repeats the same local-scope analysis.

scenario: A review criterion reads: 'Flag a comment whenever the code near it was changed in this PR.' This is explicit and unambiguous, yet the false-positive rate remains high.
stem: What is the actual problem with this criterion?

options.text: It isn't explicit enough; it needs to be made even more precise in wording.
It is explicit, but it targets the wrong condition — code being changed nearby says nothing about whether the comment's claim now contradicts the code, which is the condition that actually matters.
Explicit criteria are inherently unreliable regardless of what they specify.
The criterion needs a confidence threshold added on top of it.

rationale.correct: Explicitness alone isn't sufficient — the criterion must also target the condition that actually determines correctness. 'Code changed nearby' is a proxy that doesn't test whether the comment is now wrong; a criterion tied to actual contradiction between the comment's claim and the code's behavior is what the check needs.

distractors.A: The wording is already unambiguous; the flaw is which condition it tests, not how precisely it's phrased.
distractors.C: Explicit criteria work when they test the right condition, as established elsewhere in this exam guide; the failure here is a poorly chosen condition, not the approach itself.
distractors.D: A confidence threshold doesn't fix a criterion that's checking the wrong thing in the first place.

scenario: A style-suggestions category was temporarily disabled for a 60% false-positive rate. After adding explicit criteria, a two-week trial on historical PRs shows a 12% false-positive rate.
stem: What should determine whether it's safe to re-enable the category now?

options.text: Re-enable immediately, since any measured improvement is sufficient regardless of the new rate.

Compare the new false-positive rate against the accurate categories' existing rates (and any threshold the team considers acceptable) before re-enabling, rather than re-enabling on the basis of improvement alone.
Never re-enable a category that was ever disabled, regardless of subsequent fixes.
Re-enable it only after removing the other, already-accurate categories, to isolate its effect.

rationale.correct: Improvement alone doesn't establish that a rate is now acceptable — the right precondition is comparing the new rate against a concrete bar (the trusted categories' own rates, or an explicit acceptance threshold), not just noting that it went down from where it was.

distractors.A: Improvement without a defined bar for 'good enough' risks re-enabling a still-too-noisy category and re-eroding trust.
distractors.C: A category can legitimately be fixed and re-enabled; treating disablement as permanent discards real remediation work.
distractors.D: Removing the accurate categories has nothing to do with validating whether the fixed category is now trustworthy on its own.

scenario: A third workflow generates a weekly summary digest emailed to stakeholders every Monday morning; the job currently starts Sunday night and nobody is waiting on it in real time, but stakeholders do expect it delivered reliably by a specific hour.
stem: Is this workflow a good fit for the Message Batches API, alongside the already-agreed overnight report?

options.text: No — any deadline at all, even a next-morning one with slack, disqualifies a workflow from batch processing.

Yes — there is no one waiting on it interactively, and starting the batch with enough lead time before the deadline (accounting for batch's up-to-24-hour processing window) comfortably meets a Monday-morning delivery expectation.
Yes, but only if the batch is submitted at the exact moment the deadline begins, regardless of the up-to-24-hour processing window.
No — weekly-cadence jobs are never appropriate for the Batches API, regardless of latency tolerance.

rationale.correct: The relevant distinction is whether anyone is blocked waiting on the result in real time, not the mere existence of a deadline. Submitted with enough lead time relative to batch's up-to-24-hour window, this latency-tolerant, non-interactive workflow fits the same profile as the already-agreed overnight report.

distractors.A: A deadline with slack is exactly what batch handles well; it's tight, blocking deadlines that are the disqualifying case.
distractors.C: Submitting right at the deadline ignores the up-to-24-hour window and risks missing the delivery time; lead time is required, not optional.
distractors.D: Cadence (weekly vs. nightly) isn't the deciding factor; latency tolerance and the absence of a blocking wait are.

scenario: A CI review already avoids repeating unaddressed prior findings by passing them into context. Developers now report the reviewer still occasionally re-flags an issue that was, in fact, already fixed in the latest commit.
stem: What refinement addresses this remaining gap?

options.text: Pass the prior findings into context along with the current diff, so the model can check each prior finding against the latest code and drop any it can confirm is now resolved, not just avoid restating them blindly.
Stop passing prior findings into context altogether, since that was clearly the source of the problem.
Manually maintain a separate resolved-issues list that a human updates by hand after every fix.
Increase the context window so more history fits, without changing how findings are evaluated against the current diff.

rationale.correct: The remaining gap is that avoiding restatement isn't the same as verifying resolution — the model needs to actually re-check each prior finding against the current diff and confirm whether it still applies, not simply carry it forward unless told otherwise.

distractors.B: Removing prior context reintroduces the original duplicate-comment problem this design was built to solve.
distractors.C: A manually maintained list defeats the purpose of an automated review and adds ongoing human overhead.
distractors.D: More context alone doesn't instruct the model to actively re-verify each finding against the latest diff; that's a prompting/behavior change, not a capacity change.

scenario: CI-generated tests are low-value and ignore a project's established fixtures and testing standards.
stem: What most improves generation quality?

options.text: Increase max_tokens so more tests are generated.
Document testing standards, valuable-test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md so CI-invoked Claude uses them.
Switch test generation to the Message Batches API.
Ask for more tests per run.

rationale.correct: CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for supplying project context — standards, fixtures, and criteria — to CI-invoked Claude, which raises test quality rather than just volume.

distractors.A: More tokens increases how much can be generated, not whether it's actually valuable.
distractors.C: Batch processing affects cost and latency, not test relevance or quality.
distractors.D: Asking for more tests per run increases volume in the same way option A does, without addressing quality.

scenario: In a batch of 500 jobs, 12 fail due to oversized documents (fixable by chunking) and 3 fail because the source PDF is corrupted and won't open at all.
stem: How should the recovery differ between these two failure groups?

options.text: Treat all 15 identically: chunk every failed document and resubmit all 15 using their custom_ids.

Resubmit the 12 oversized documents after chunking them; the 3 corrupted files can't be chunked into a valid document and need to be re-sourced (or flagged for manual attention) before any resubmission makes sense.
Discard all 15 failures and accept the loss, since any failure in a large batch is expected.
Resubmit the entire batch of 500, since distinguishing failure types adds unnecessary complexity.

rationale.correct: The two failure types need different remediation: chunking fixes an oversized-but-otherwise-valid document, but a corrupted file has no valid content to chunk — it needs a new source file (or human attention) before resubmission is even possible. custom_id still lets you target exactly these 15 without touching the 485 that succeeded.

distractors.A: Chunking a corrupted file that won't open produces nothing usable; the two failure classes need genuinely different fixes.
distractors.C: Discarding recoverable failures (the 12 oversized ones, at least) wastes work that a straightforward fix would have salvaged.
distractors.D: Resubmitting all 500 wastes cost reprocessing 485 jobs that already succeeded, and still wouldn't fix the corrupted files.

scenario: A pipeline uses tool_use with a JSON schema requiring line_items to be a non-empty array of {sku, quantity} objects. Extractions are always syntactically valid JSON conforming to that shape, yet some invoices come back with zero line items even though the source document clearly lists several.
stem: What does this indicate, and is it addressed by tool_use's schema guarantee?

options.text: Since output is always schema-valid, this is not a problem tool_use can address at all, and nothing further should be done.

The schema guarantees structural validity (a well-formed array of the right shape) but not that the array's contents are complete or accurate — that's a semantic completeness issue requiring its own check, such as validating line-item count against other invoice fields.
The schema itself is broken and must be rewritten to require a minimum array length before this can be diagnosed.
Switching to a larger model will resolve completeness regardless of the schema.

rationale.correct: tool_use enforces structural conformance — the array's shape is valid — but has no way to guarantee the array's contents are complete or correct. Missing line items despite a valid empty (or under-filled) array is a semantic completeness problem, which needs an explicit downstream check, not a schema-shape fix.

distractors.A: The gap is real and addressable — just not through the schema-conformance mechanism alone; a completeness check is the appropriate addition.
distractors.C: A minimum-length constraint could force a non-empty array but wouldn't guarantee the array's contents are the correct items — it would risk the model padding with placeholder values instead.
distractors.D: Model size doesn't address a structural/procedural gap in what's being validated; a completeness check does.

scenario: An invoice_number field is present on most invoices but genuinely absent on a minority of internal transfer documents. When present, it must always match the pattern INV-\d{6}.
stem: How should the schema be designed to prevent both fabrication and format drift?

options.text: Require the field always, format-constrained, forcing the model to invent a plausible-looking value for the documents that lack one.
Make the field nullable, and apply the format pattern constraint only to non-null values, so absence is representable and any present value must still conform.
Make the field a free-text string with no pattern constraint, to avoid ever rejecting a real but unusually-formatted value.
Drop the field from the schema entirely, since it isn't present on every document type.

rationale.correct: Nullable handles genuine absence without fabrication pressure, and a format constraint that only applies to non-null values preserves that the field's shape is guaranteed whenever it actually exists — combining both concerns rather than trading one off against the other.

distractors.A: Requiring the field forces exactly the fabrication this design is meant to prevent, for the documents that legitimately lack one.
distractors.C: Dropping the format constraint entirely lets genuinely malformed values through even when the field is present, undermining downstream use of the field.
distractors.D: Removing the field entirely discards a field that IS meaningful and extractable on the majority of documents that do have it.

scenario: Beyond document_type (five known values plus new/ambiguous cases), each document also needs a sub_category whose valid values depend on which document_type was assigned, and new sub-categories appear even more often than new document types.
stem: How should the schema handle the dependent, even-more-volatile sub_category field?

options.text: Use the same enum-plus-other-plus-unclear pattern for sub_category as for document_type, independent of the two fields' different volatility.

Since sub_category is more volatile and depends on document_type, keep the same other-with-detail-string fallback but expect it to be exercised more frequently, and treat document_type as authoritative context for interpreting the other value rather than requiring sub_category's enum to anticipate every combination up front.
Make sub_category a required field with no fallback at all, since it's clearly the more important field.
Merge document_type and sub_category into a single combined enum listing every valid pairing in advance.

rationale.correct: The same extensible pattern still applies, but recognizing that sub_category is more volatile means expecting the fallback path to carry more real cases, and using the already-known document_type as context to interpret an 'other' sub_category avoids trying to pre-enumerate every future pairing.

distractors.A: Applying the pattern identically without accounting for the different volatility and the dependency between the two fields misses the actual design challenge in this scenario.
distractors.C: A required field with no fallback for the more volatile of the two fields is the fabrication-risk pattern this whole approach exists to avoid.
distractors.D: Pre-enumerating every valid pairing defeats the purpose of an extensible design for a field that changes more often than the other.

scenario: Your extraction schema defines `invoice_total` as a number, but the model sometimes returns it as the string "$1,240.00" instead of the numeric value 1240.00, even though the surrounding fields validate fine.
stem: What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Add explicit normalization guidance and a worked input/output example (stripping currency symbols and commas, then coercing to a number) so the model reliably emits the correctly-typed value.
Loosen the schema so `invoice_total` accepts either a string or a number, and normalize downstream in application code.
Reject the whole extraction and ask a human to retype the number.
Increase `max_tokens` so the model has more room to format the number correctly.

rationale.correct: This is a formatting/normalization issue the model can reliably fix once shown exactly what's expected — a concrete input/output example demonstrating the currency-string-to-number transformation is the most direct, low-effort fix.

distractors.B: Loosening the schema to accept either type pushes the normalization problem downstream instead of fixing it, and reintroduces exactly the inconsistency structured extraction is meant to eliminate.
distractors.C: Discarding a mostly-correct extraction over one fixable formatting issue is disproportionate.
distractors.D: More tokens doesn't address a formatting/type convention the model simply hasn't been shown clearly.

scenario: An extraction attempt fails validation for two independent reasons at once: a malformed date and a missing required field that genuinely is present in the source document.
stem: How should the retry-with-error-feedback request be constructed?

options.text: Send only the date error first, then retry a second time for the missing field once the date is fixed, one issue per retry.
Include both validation errors in the same retry request alongside the original document and failed output, so the model can address both in one pass.
Discard the attempt and skip straight to human review, since two simultaneous errors indicate the case is too complex to retry.
Retry with the date error only, and silently drop the missing-required-field error since it will likely resolve on its own.

rationale.correct: Since both are independent, fixable, structural/format issues, surfacing both validation errors together in one retry lets the model correct them in a single pass — sequencing them across separate retries adds unnecessary round-trips for problems that don't depend on each other.

distractors.A: Splitting genuinely independent, fixable errors across sequential retries costs an extra round-trip for no benefit.
distractors.C: Two structural errors are still within retry-with-feedback's wheelhouse; escalating to human review is premature when both are correctable format/completeness issues.
distractors.D: Silently dropping a real validation error risks shipping data that's still wrong; it should be surfaced, not ignored.

scenario: An extraction pipeline processes only page 1 of a multi-page contract PDF. The governing_law field is required and comes back null, but the clause actually appears on page 3.
stem: Is this the same 'retry won't help' situation as information that is genuinely absent from the source, or something else?

options.text: The same situation — retries never help with a missing field, regardless of cause, so the fix is to make the field nullable and move on.

A different situation — the information exists in the source but wasn't supplied to the model at all; the fix is to include page 3 in the extraction input, after which a retry (or the original request, resubmitted with full input) can succeed.
The same situation — since page 1 alone was given, the model correctly determined the field is absent, and no further input would change that.
A different situation, but unfixable — multi-page contracts should be excluded from extraction entirely.

rationale.correct: This differs from true absence: the data exists in the source, it just wasn't included in what the model was given. Unlike a field that's genuinely missing from the document, this is fixed by supplying the missing page, not by accepting null or escalating to a human.

distractors.A: This isn't the genuinely-absent case; treating it identically would accept a null that a fuller input could actually resolve.
distractors.C: The model didn't determine anything about page 3 at all — it was never given that page, which is different from having reviewed the full document and finding no such clause.
distractors.D: Excluding an entire document category is a disproportionate response to an input-scoping bug that has a direct fix.

scenario: A team is ready to segment their 97%-aggregate extraction accuracy figure but is unsure which breakdowns are worth computing first, given limited analysis time.
stem: Which breakdowns are most likely to reveal a masked problem, and why?

options.text: Only a breakdown by the day of the week the document was processed, since accuracy could plausibly vary by processing schedule.

Breakdowns by document type and by individual field, since aggregate accuracy is a volume-weighted average that can hide a minority document type or a specific field performing far worse than the overall number suggests.
Only a breakdown by which team member configured the extraction pipeline, since human factors are the most likely hidden variable.
No breakdown is more informative than another; any single cut is equally likely to reveal a problem.

rationale.correct: Document type and field are the dimensions where a volume-weighted aggregate is most likely to mask trouble: a low-volume document type or a specific field can perform far worse than the aggregate suggests while barely moving the overall number. Processing day or configurer identity aren't the mechanisms this masking effect actually depends on.

distractors.A: Day-of-week isn't the dimension the volume-weighting masking effect operates on; it's a plausible but much lower-value first cut than type/field.
distractors.C: Configurer identity isn't established as a relevant factor here and isn't where the volume-weighting effect hides problems.
distractors.D: Not all cuts are equally informative; type and field are specifically where a volume-weighted aggregate is known to mask segment-level problems.

scenario: A team wants to calibrate field-level confidence scores against labeled data to drive review routing, but only has 200 labeled examples so far, far fewer than they'd like.
stem: What is the most reasonable way to proceed given the limited labeled set?

options.text: Skip calibration entirely and route based on raw model-reported confidence until a much larger labeled set exists.

Use the 200 examples for an initial calibration, treat it as provisional, and expand the labeled set over time (e.g., by continuing to sample and label extractions) to refine the calibration as more data accumulates.
Wait until a labeled set of at least several thousand examples exists before doing any calibration work at all.
Use the 200 examples to calibrate once, and never revisit the calibration regardless of how much more labeled data becomes available later.

rationale.correct: An initial, provisional calibration from the available data is more useful than none, as long as it's treated as a starting point to refine as the labeled set grows — this avoids both the unreliability of uncalibrated raw confidence and an indefinite wait for a large labeled set before doing anything.

distractors.A: Uncalibrated raw confidence is exactly the unreliable signal calibration is meant to fix; using it by default while waiting isn't the better option.
distractors.C: Waiting for a large labeled set before any calibration work defers a usable improvement for no clear benefit over a provisional, refinable calibration.
distractors.D: Treating an early calibration as permanent ignores that more labeled data becoming available is a reason to refine it, not a fact to ignore.
